sentences.text: He asked at home and got the answer people give.
His mother said there was probably a nest of something.
His father said the same and added that the field had been left three years and was full of voles and that a bird over a field was not news.

His sister, who was nineteen and studying something with animals in it and who was therefore insufferable that year, said that kestrels absolutely do repeat productive patches and that Tomás had discovered nothing.
She was right, as it happens, about the general case.
That is what makes the argument worth reporting.
Kestrels do repeat productive patches.
They will work a good verge for weeks.

Everything his sister said at that table was correct as a statement about kestrels, and it was delivered with the total confidence of somebody in the second year of a degree, and it was very nearly the reason Tomás dropped the whole thing.
He has thought about that more than about any other part of it.
She had better information than he did.
She had actual training.

And what she did with the better information was use it to explain away an observation she had not made, about a field she had not looked at, because the observation had come from her thirteen-year-old brother.
He went back on the Thursday mostly out of spite.
He would like to be able to claim a better reason and there was not one.
He went back on the Thursday.
She was there.
Same corner.
Same height, which he had started estimating and had settled at about twelve metres.
He watched her for half an hour this time and counted.
He had brought a watch and a notebook, having decided overnight to be serious about it, and he sat on the verge with the bike laid over in the grass and did the thing properly.
In thirty-one minutes she came down twice — properly stooped, dropped feet-first into the stubble — and came up twice with nothing, and went straight back to the same place and hung again.
That was the part that undid the vole theory.
A kestrel that misses moves.
It is not sentimental about a patch.
Two misses in half an hour on the fourth day and she was still there.
He worked out the rest of it on the way home, standing on the pedals up the hill.
Hovering costs.

He did not have the number, but he did not need the number; he had watched her do it for thirty-one minutes without a break longer than a few seconds, and anything that looks that much like hard work is hard work.
A bird does not spend four days doing the most expensive thing it can do over a patch of stubble the size of a garage because it is fond of the view.
Either there was something there worth four days, or she was broken.
And she was plainly not broken.
She was hovering beautifully — better, if anything, than the ones he saw over the motorway, holding position in a crosswind that was pushing the thistles about.
So there was something there.
He had been looking at the wrong part of the field for three days.
He had been looking at the grass, because the grass is where a vole is.
He had not once looked at the concrete.
He said this at dinner, with numbers, and his sister said that was actually interesting, in the tone of somebody surprised to be saying it.
His father put his fork down.
"Fourth day." "Fourth." "Which corner?" "The one by the road.
Where the shed was." His father looked at the table for a moment and then said, "Ask Old Vasco."
